analysis.title: Powering AI: The modular advantage - how value shifts and who captures it
key_insights: Construction is replacing power availability as the binding constraint on data center deployment. Moving work from field to factory (modularisation) can cut deployment time by 30-60% and ease the MEP labour bottleneck.

Modularisation shifts procurement from individual products to integrated systems, expanding content per MW and creating share-gain opportunities for vertically integrated OEMs. Bernstein names Schneider, Vertiv and Eaton as best positioned.

Behind-the-meter (BTM) power is 22% of data center projects under construction and 40% of the pipeline, versus 6% of active data centers. US interconnection timelines rose from 1.5 years in 2005 to over 5 years in 2025.
Crusoe indicates data center construction still takes 18-24 months after switching to BTM power, with physical construction and installation over 15 months of that.

Bernstein's US Electrical Equipment team sees an MEP labour ceiling of up to 35 GW of US data center additions by 2030. A GPU-manufacturing-implied ceiling is roughly double at 70 GW, though it includes retrofits.
800 VDC architecture raises MEP fit-out labour hours by about 50% initially, per a channel check with an MEP estimator. 70% of projects are in regions with only 30% of the MEP labour pool.

OEM lead-time claims for modular: Schneider 88 weeks stick-built down to 34 weeks, Vertiv 10 weeks on site with modular versus 70 weeks otherwise, ABB 50% reduction in deployment time. Schneider, ABB and Vertiv expect lead times to compress by about 60% on average.

Modular share of additions is about 40% today, up from about 30% in 2023, and Bernstein expects just under 60% by 2030. Modular additions grow at a 24% CAGR versus 14% for the market, about 10pp faster.

Non-hyperscaler customers (neoclouds, crypto miners, colos) are expected to drive 60% of 2026-2030 additions versus about 40% over 2023-2025. They are assumed to adopt modular faster. Survey subsamples are small (n=5 each for colos and neoclouds).
Bernstein models about 3pp of net market share gain for the best-positioned vertically integrated OEMs. This assumes the OEM can supply 80-90% of module content internally.
Addressable market is $1.9B/GW for Power modules and $1.8B/GW for IT modules. Halving a 30-month deployment is worth about $0.9B/GW of present value, with about $0.2B/GW (about 25%) captured by OEMs.
Modularisation could cut MEP labour costs by about 37%, driven by a 58% cut in electrical labour. Bernstein uses Schneider's time savings as a proxy for labour hours.

Margins: near-term EBITA/MW is a slight positive, as pricing and content gains are partly offset by capacity ramp-up costs, discounting and higher selling costs. Mid-to-long-term EBITA/MW is a strong positive from standardisation, factory scale and SG&A and R&D leverage.
Larger, earlier orders and faster backlog conversion should improve earnings visibility. Prefab cuts deployment time by about 30% and predesign by an incremental 20%.
Schneider has the most proven customer wins and the broadest product coverage. It has added prefab capacity of over 1M sqft (+270% in 2 years) and partners with Foxconn, Compass and Switch.

Vertiv stands out for its ambitious strategy: SmartRun IT pods scaling from 1.5MW to over 6MW (Schneider tops out at 1.2MW), and OneCore architecture from 12.5MW to a 1GW campus. Bernstein notes higher project risk, citing VRT's Q2'26 results as showing supply chain teething issues.
Eaton has strengthened its offering via the Fibrebond acquisition (Apr'25) and a Flexnode partnership (Jan'26). Its own-brand IT pod offering lags Schneider and Vertiv in maturity.

Legrand, ABB and Siemens are in the narrower 'distributed' camp and are disadvantaged unless they integrate further. Legrand could assemble a full offering (Girtz acquisition Jun'26, grey space exposure up from under 1% of 2023 sales to about 8% in H1'26). ABB lacks an IT pod. Siemens relies on partnerships (Delta, Cadolto/Legrand).

Proprietary survey (n=50): 52% prefer both Power and IT pods for future AI deployments, 32% prefer one of the two, and 16% prefer stick-built. Single-sourcing is the current preference of 38% of respondents. Respondents expect modular to raise single-sourcing willingness.

Aug'26 Bernstein survey (n=50): a quarter of respondents report lead times rising over 20% year on year across 13 equipment categories. Jul'26 DCD survey (n=88) ranks equipment lead times first among delivery constraints (24%).
Consensus hyperscaler and neocloud capex is $823B in 2026e, rising to $1,391B by 2030e per Exhibit 12.

Stand-out ambitious modular strategy (SmartRun over 6MW, OneCore to 1GW campuses). Higher project risk is flagged, with Q2'26 supply chain issues cited.
Improved modular position through acquisitions and partnerships but less mature than Schneider and Vertiv.
Could become a compelling integrated provider post-Girtz but currently risks being left behind by integrated module providers.

Relies on partnerships to fill portfolio gaps, which dilutes modular upside.

sector_views.rationale: Modularisation expands content per MW, improves order visibility and backlog conversion, and favours vertically integrated OEMs (Schneider, Vertiv, Eaton) over narrower portfolios.

earnings_insights: Vertiv Q2'26 results are cited as showing the impact of internal and external supply chain teething issues on integrated modular project execution. No figures given.

Near-term EBITA/MW effects of modularisation are slight positive. Pricing and content gains are partly offset by capacity ramp-up costs and higher selling costs. Longer term it is a strong positive from SG&A and R&D leverage.

Bernstein Ticker Table adjusted EPS (2025A/2026E/2027E): Schneider EUR 8.43/10.42/13.24, Vertiv $4.20/6.60/9.06, Eaton $12.07/13.45/16.37. These are Bernstein estimates for 2026E and 2027E; Siemens and GEV are reported EPS.

macro_indicators.indicator: US interconnection request to commercial operation, median time
macro_indicators.interpretation: Grid access delays push data center developers toward behind-the-meter power and now modular construction.
Consensus spending trajectory used to phase Bernstein's 126 GW credible data center additions.

crypto_views: Crypto miners are included among non-hyperscaler data center customers that are speed-oriented and more likely to prefer OEM-led standardised modular platforms.
Crypto developers have a high share of pipeline using behind-the-meter power (Exhibit 11).

trade_ideas.description: Favour integrated modular OEMs Schneider, Vertiv and Eaton over narrower portfolios at Legrand, ABB and Siemens
trade_ideas.rationale: Modular shift consolidates procurement at module level and gives integrated OEMs about 3pp of net share gain.
trade_ideas.risk: Higher project risk and supply chain exposure for vertically integrated providers; near-term margin dilution from ramp-up and selling costs.

risk_factors: Higher project risk for vertically integrated OEMs delivering whole facilities, with exposure to third-party supply chain issues (Vertiv Q2'26 cited).
Near-term margin benefits may be diluted by capacity ramp-up costs, discounting and bundling to win sales of unproven modules, and higher selling costs.
Turnkey contractor role exposes OEMs to third-party pricing and logistics risk.
Survey sample sizes are small (n=5 for colos and neoclouds), limiting conclusions on adoption by customer type.
Hyperscalers may prefer to retain design authority and use EPCs, with about 10% still preferring stick-built.
Hyperscaler capex through 2030 is a moving target and an imperfect proxy for data center addition phasing.
Single-sourcing remains only 38% of current preferences, so the market is still fragmented by design.
Other constraints on build-out remain (energisation, AI chips), and the thesis assumes demand stays high.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 plots deployment time in years: grid connection 5-7, heavy-duty gas turbines 4-5, aero 2-3, industrial about 2, engines 1-2, fuel cells 0-1, stick-built construction 1.5-2, modular 0.5-1.
Exhibit 7 shows median US interconnection request to commercial operation time rising from 1.5 years in 2005 to 5.1 years in 2025, a widening of over 3x or 6% per year.
Exhibit 10 shows behind-the-meter share of projects by stage as 6% active, 22% construction and 40% pipeline.
Exhibit 17 shows YTD price return of Bloom Energy 191%, GE Vernova 44% and S&P 500 Industrials 13%.
Exhibit 33 shows credibility-adjusted data center additions from 4.1 GW in 2023 to 29.1 GW in 2030, with modular share rising from 30.0% to 56.9%.
Exhibit 38 shows implied MEP labour cost falling from $7.50B/GW to $4.76B/GW (-37%), with electrical labour down 58%.
geopolitical: Bernstein notes the gap between US and Chinese AI models on Epoch AI benchmarks has widened since the early 2025 'DeepSeek moment', but cheaper releases such as Kimi K3 mean the US must invest heavily to stay ahead.
BNEF data shows China added about 635 GW of generation capacity in 2025, over 40% of total US installed capacity.

tension_points.bull_case: Modular cuts deployment time 30-60%, eases MEP labour limits and lifts modular share from about 40% to about 57% of additions by 2030, giving integrated OEMs about 3pp of share gain and higher EBITA/MW.
tension_points.bear_case: Near-term gains are diluted by ramp-up and selling costs, and integrated providers take on higher project risk (Vertiv Q2'26 supply chain issues). Hyperscalers may keep design authority and use EPCs, and single-sourcing is only 38% of current preference.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Hyperscalers staying with EPC-led stick-built execution, or modular penetration failing to rise toward 57% by 2030 (the report says survey subsamples for colos and neoclouds are small, n=5 each).

theme_stances.key_argument: Modularisation bypasses EPC delays and scarce MEP labour, shifts procurement toward integrated systems and benefits vertically integrated OEMs.
theme_stances.evidence: Modularisation is becoming the next critical lever in accelerating data center deployment

theme_stances.key_argument: Integrated providers Schneider, Vertiv and Eaton offer the clearest covered exposure, while Legrand, ABB and Siemens have narrower portfolios.
theme_stances.evidence: Integrated providers Schneider, Vertiv, and Eaton offer the clearest covered exposure
